summary: Number-theory and counting problems: nCr under a modulus, Pascal's triangle, digit counting, and base conversions (Excel columns are base-26). The recurring traps are integer overflow and doing division under a modulus. Build combinations with Pascal's recurrence or factorials + modular inverse; count by place value; treat Excel columns as 1-indexed base-26 with no zero digit.

thoughtProcess.title: Is the answer under a modulus? Then never divide — multiply by the modular inverse.
thoughtProcess.body: a/b % m is NOT (a%m)/(b%m). Under a prime modulus, divide by b == multiply by b^(m-2) (Fermat). For nCr%p either precompute factorials + inverse factorials, or build Pascal's triangle where every step is only addition (no division needed).

thoughtProcess.title: Excel columns are base-26 but 1-indexed (A=1..Z=26), with no zero.
thoughtProcess.body: Converting number->title, subtract 1 each step: c = (n-1)%26 -> letter, n=(n-1)/26. Title->number is plain Horner base-26: n = n*26 + (ch-'A'+1). Forgetting the -1 shifts every letter.

thoughtProcess.title: Counting 'how many X in [1..N]'? Count per place / per block, don't enumerate.
thoughtProcess.body: Number of Digit One, Consecutive Numbers Sum, permutation rank — all count contributions by digit position or by factor, in O(log N) or O(sqrt N), never by looping to N (which TLEs at N=1e9).

keyPatterns.name: nCr % p via Pascal (addition only)
keyPatterns.when: Small n (<= a few thousand); avoids modular inverse

keyPatterns.name: Base-26 (Excel column) conversion
keyPatterns.template:
title: while n>0: n--; sb.append('A'+n%26); n/=26; reverse
number: for ch: n = n*26 + (ch-'A'+1)

keyPatterns.name: Digit / place-value counting
keyPatterns.when: Count a property over [1..N] without iterating
keyPatterns.template: for place = 1,10,100..: derive count from high/cur/low digits

commonMistakes.title: Dividing under a modulus
commonMistakes.right: ans = nFact % p * modpow(rFact, p-2, p) % p * modpow((n-r)Fact, p-2, p) % p;
commonMistakes.why: Integer division loses the remainder and is invalid under a modulus. Use the modular inverse (Fermat, p prime) or Pascal's addition-only recurrence.

commonMistakes.title: int overflow in factorial / products
commonMistakes.wrong: int f = 1; for k: f *= k;
commonMistakes.right: long f = 1; for k: f = f * k % MOD;
commonMistakes.why: 21! overflows even long; a*b for a,b ~1e9 overflows int. Use long and reduce % MOD after every multiply.

edgeCases: nCr with r > n -> 0; r == 0 or r == n -> 1 (guard before indexing factorial arrays).
Excel Column Title: the -1 before %/ is what makes 26 -> 'Z' and 27 -> 'AA'; without it you get 'A@' style bugs.
Use long for the place multiplier loop in Number of Digit One: i*10 and high*i overflow int at the top powers of ten (10^9), even though 10^9 itself fits in int.
Intermediate values need long: k*(k-1)/2 and the remainder in consecutive-sum, and factorial products (smaller*fact) in permutation-rank. The final counts themselves fit in int.
